entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂ep- 'water, body of water' (Mallory & Adams 1997 *h₂eb(h)-); Wiktionary's reconstruction unifies an Italo-Celtic branch (*h₂ph₃n-éh₂ > Lat. amnis, Proto-Celtic *abū) with the Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́ps branch (Av./Skt ap-). Pokorny (1959) instead splits these into two separate headwords: 'ab- "Wasser, Fluß"' (p.1, Italo-Celtic) and '2. äp- "Wasser, Fluß"' (p.51, Indo-Iranian/Greek, = AHD's ap-2, Pok. 51).
entries.note: Nourai's box groups 'Ab' and 'Ap' as one root and cites only POK:1, but the branch actually drawn in this chart (Avestan/Pahlavi āp > Persian āb) belongs to Pokorny's separate entry '2. äp-' on p.51 (AHD: 'ap-2. Water, river. Iranian ap- in Persian ab, water: JULEP. [Pok. 2. ap- 51.]'), not to the p.1 'ab-' entry (Latin amnis, Old Irish ab, Celtic river names). Pokorny's own p.1 entry does cross-reference the p.51 entry ('Vgl. auch 2. äp- "Wasser, Fluß"'), and modern IE comparative work (Mallory & Adams 1997, followed by Wiktionary's *h₂ep- reconstruction) treats both as suffixed extensions of one root, so grouping them is defensible, but the specific page citation POK:1 does not cover the Iranian material illustrated by the nodes below.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaf 9 (printed p.1): "ab- „Wasser, Fluß“. Lat. amnis ... air. ab Gen. ahae ... Vgl. auch 2. up- [sic, = äp-] „Wasser, Fluß“ und abö(n) 'Affe'." This p.1 entry is the Italo-Celtic 'river' word (Latin amnis, Old Irish ab); it only cross-references, but does not itself contain, the Indo-Iranian material (Skt/Av. ap-) that the chart's nodes actually illustrate. That material is Pokorny's separate entry '2. äp- „Wasser, Fluß“' at printed p.51 (POK_01.txt leaf 60): 'Ai. áp- f. Wasser ... av. Nom. Sg. āfš, Akk. Sg. āpąm ...'.

consulted.note: '2. äp-, Wasser, Fluß': Ai. áp- f. 'water', av. Nom.Sg. āfš, Akk.Sg. āpąm — exactly the Iranian branch of the chart, but cited on p.51, not p.1 as Nourai's root box gives.

"2. ap- „Wasser, Fluß“." — Walde-Pokorny also lists this as a separate, independently numbered headword parallel to Pokorny, confirming the Indo-Iranian 'water' root is treated as distinct from the Italo-Celtic 'ab-' entry.

"ap-2, Water, river. Iranian ap- in Persian ab, water: JULEP. [Pok. 2. ap- 51.]" — directly supports the Iranian branch of the chart, but its own citation is Pokorny p.51, confirming the p.1 citation on Nourai's root box is for a different (related) sub-entry.

Mann's entry for the Italo-Celtic river-word (Alb. āmë, Lat. amnis, Gaulish abono-, OIr. aba) lists no Indo-Iranian ap-/āp- cognates, i.e. keeps the two branches separate rather than uniting them under one PIE etymon.

nodes.derivation: PIE *h₂ep- 'water' > Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́ps > Proto-Iranian *Hā́fš. Old Avestan apō (acc.pl.); Younger Avestan ap- (nom./obl. stem), āfš (nom.sg., with the expected Iranian cluster development -ps- > -fš-); Old Persian api(y)a- (transferred to an i-stem, e.g. loc.sg. apiyā); Middle Persian (Manichaean) āb, Book Pahlavi ʾp' = āb, all continuing simple regular loss of the earlier consonant cluster with compensatory lengthening/simplification to -b-. Meaning 'water' is unbroken from PIE to New Persian āb.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 14 (printed ~p.3-4, running head 'abasia—abiogenesis', within Klein's stated +/-2 leaf-to-page tolerance of the cited p.2): s.v. 'abdest': "Pers. âbdâst, lit. 'water for the hand', fr. ab, 'water', and dast, 'hand'. Pers. ab, 'water', is rel. to Avestic âp-, OI. âpah (fem. pl.), 'water'; see amnic and cp. ... julep." — Klein explicitly states Persian āb is related to Avestan āp-, matching the node's claim.

consulted.note: Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch lists 'ap-' as the Avestan word for water with the expected paradigm (nom.pl. āpō, gen.pl. apąm etc.); no separate 'glitter' sense is given for this entry.
"ab [MYA<Amyʾ, PN)b, N.....] water." — MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary confirms Pahlavi ab/āb = 'water' only; no second homograph is listed.
Kent's Old Persian lexicon entry for api(y)a- ('water') was not directly located in the local OCR text, so no direct quote could be pulled; treated as silent rather than checked.

nodes.derivation: âb 'glitter, shine' (as distinct from âb 'water'): Nourai follows Horn (Grundriss, 1893, entry '3. äb Glanz', printed p.1), who compares Skt ābhā- 'splendor' and lists compounds âb-mand, Rūdābe, Sohrāb, Mehrāb, Ardāvirāf, âftâb as containing this 'shine' element (Phlv. āb, Skt ābhā- 'Glanz'). However Horn HIMSELF flags the equation as uncertain (footnote: 'Die Zusammenstellung von np. āb und skr. ābhā- ist keineswegs sicher; von der Bedeutung "glitzernder Wasserspiegel" könnte man sehr leicht zu "Glanz" kommen' — i.e. it is easy to get from 'glittering water-surface' to 'shine' as a plain semantic extension of āb 'water', without positing a separate etymon), and Hübschmann (Persische Studien, 1895) explicitly cites this uncertainty ('Da ab "Glanz" == skr. ābhā- H.[orn] 3 unsicher ist ...'). Modern Wiktionary and MacKenzie's Pahlavi dictionary give only one āb, 'water', with no second lexical entry for 'shine'. âberū(y) 'good reputation, honor' is transparently âb + rūy 'face' = 'water of the face' (paralleled by the Arabic idiom مَاء الوَجه māʾ al-wajh, lit. 'water of the face' = honor/shame), a semantic metaphor built on the literal 'water' sense rather than requiring a separate 'shine' root (though the metaphor of a shining/glowing face is not unreasonable either). âftâb 'sun(shine)': modern Iranology (Cheung, Etymological Dictionary of the Iranian Verb, 2007, and Wiktionary) reconstructs Middle Persian ʾptʾb (āftāb) from Proto-Iranian *abi-tāpah — i.e. the PREPOSITION *abi- 'upon, unto, towards' (cognate with Avestan aiwi-, Sanskrit api, Greek epi-, unrelated to āp 'water') + *tāpa- 'heat, glow' (from the verbal root tap- 'to be/become hot', NP tāftan/tāb-). So the modern analysis of the first element of āftāb is the preposition 'abi-/upon' plus 'heat', not āb 'water' or 'glitter' at all — the resemblance to āb is coincidental homophony of Iranian *abi- and *āp-.

ref_check.note: HRN.txt lines 464-473 (printed p.1, entry no.3): "3. äb 'Glanz' (Sahn. I S.14 Vers 7), vergl. ab[rö, ah[tah, äb[mend, Röd]äbe, Suhr]ab, Mihr]äb, Ardä VTr]af, af[täb, phlv. üb; skr. äbhä- 'Glanz'." Footnote: "Die Zusammenstellung von np. ab und skr. abhä- ist keineswegs sicher; von der Bedeutung 'glitzernder Wasserspiegel' könnte man sehr leicht zu 'Glanz' kommen." Horn's own page supports the compounds Nourai lists but explicitly marks the Skt ābhā- equation, and by extension the idea of āb 'shine' as a separate root, as unproven.

Khaleqi Motlaq's Asas-e Eshteqaq-e Farsi (Persian translation/expansion of Horn+Hübschmann) has no online copy and was not in the local corpus; per refs_online.json guidance it is proxied via HRN/HUB, both consulted above.

consulted.note: "Da ab 'Glanz' == skr. abha- H.[orn] 3 unsicher ist, so ergiebt sich, dass ap. w nur vor r sicher zu np. b wird." — Hübschmann treats the āb='Glanz' equation as unconfirmed ('unsicher') and uses that very uncertainty as an argument elsewhere in his sound-law discussion; he does not endorse it as settled.
Only one Pahlavi entry 'ab...water' is given; no second homograph meaning 'shine/glitter' appears in MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary.
"NWIR: NP taftan/tab- 'to shine, burn' ... || (+ *abi-) NP āftāb 'sun(shine)'" — Cheung derives NP āftāb from tap- 'to shine, burn' plus the prefix *abi- ('upon'), not from āb 'water/glitter'.

Immediately preceding entry (no.2, also printed p.1): "ab, âw 'Wasser'; ... ap. āp- 'Wasser'; aw. āp-; phlv. āp (pāz. āw); ai. āp-, kurd. āw ..." — this is Horn's WATER entry (matching node #1); the 'Glanz' sense is a separately numbered, admittedly uncertain, homograph (entry no.3).

nodes.derivation: Nourai proposes that Arabic أبّهة/أُبَّهة (ubbuha/ubbaha 'pomp, majesty, grandeur') arose from a Persian-Arabic hybrid compound 'āb' (glitter) + 'bahā'' (Arabic 'splendor'), i.e. treating it as an Arabized borrowing of a Persian phrase. Modern Arabic lexicography does not support this: Wiktionary lists أبهة under the native triliteral root ء ب ه (ʔ-b-h), from the plain Arabic verb أَبَهَ/أَبِهَ (ʔabaha/ʔabiha) 'to pay attention, heed, take notice' (non-past يَأْبَهُ yaʔbahu); أُبَّهة is the augmented/intensive noun pattern of that root (gemination marking intensity: roughly 'that which makes one take notice' → pomp, ostentatious grandeur). This root (ء ب ه) is listed as entirely separate from ب ه و / ب ه ي, the root of بَهَاء (bahāʔ) 'splendor, beauty' (which Klein's Comprehensive Etymological Dictionary treats as the source of Persian 'bahā' splendor', via 'Bahaism' < Pers. bahā < Arab. bahāʔ — i.e. the borrowing runs Arabic→Persian for bahāʔ itself, not the reverse). There is no attested classical or modern source deriving أبهة from a Persian 'āb' + Arabic 'bahā'' compound; the resemblance between 'ubbuha' and 'āb-bahā' appears to be a folk/paronomastic etymology rather than an attested derivation.

ref_check.note: AFM_pages.txt around leaf 13-17 (approx. printed pp.5-9 per the −8 leaf offset, transitioning from bāb al-alif to bāb al-bāʾ) was inspected but the Arabic-script OCR is too degraded (Syriac-looking mis-OCR of Arabic letters) to locate or confirm an entry for أبهة/عبهة at p.7; could not verify Nourai's claim against this source.
Emam Shushtari's Farhang-e Vazheha-ye Farsi dar Zaban-e Arabi has no local OCR text and is only available behind login/JS-gated viewers (noorlib.ir, ketabnak.com); could not be fetched.

consulted.note: "Bahaism, n. ... Formed with suff. -ism fr. Pers. baha, 'splendor', fr. Arab. bahā', of s.m." — Klein derives Persian 'bahā' FROM Arabic bahāʔ (opposite direction of loan from what a Persian-origin compound in Arabic 'ubbuha' would require), and gives no compound with āb.
Jeffery's Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur'an (Quranic loanwords only) has no entry for أبهة/بهاء (neither word is Qur'anic vocabulary), so it is silent on this claim.
No entry found relating أبهة or بهاء to an Aramaic substrate; silent.

nodes.derivation: New Persian ابهت (conventionally vocalized ebhat/obhat/obbohat) 'grandeur, majesty, awe' is a straightforward Arabic loanword from أُبَّهة (ubbuha/ubbaha) 'pomp, majesty' (see node 3), following the common pattern of Arabic feminine nouns in -a(t) being borrowed into Persian with the historical tāʾ marbūṭa retained as -at/-et (cf. Ar. -a(t) > NP -at in many loans). Mo'in's Farhang-e Farsi (MON) explicitly tags the word's origin as Arabic, and the meaning given there ('bozorgi, bozorgvāri, azamat' = grandeur, magnificence; also 'tokabbor, nakhvat' = arrogance/pride) matches Nourai's gloss 'elegance/magnificence'. The Persian←Arabic borrowing direction for this specific word (node 3→node 4 edge) is correctly drawn and uncontroversial; the caveat is only about the deeper origin Nourai assigns to the Arabic word itself at node 3 (see there).
